name: HPTT (High-Performance Tensor Transposition)
baseline: numpy.transpose (np.transpose(A, perm).copy(order=order), as timed in pythonAPI/benchmark/benchmark.py)
workload: Out-of-place float32 tensor transposition (with optional alpha/beta update for HPTT) over about 57 permutation/size test cases, HPTT with 24 threads versus numpy; bandwidth in GiB/s, minimum of 5 runs with the cache flushed between runs.
claimed_speedup: README figure hptt_vs_numpy.png (bar chart, no table): speedup over numpy.transpose of roughly 5x to 20x per test case (lowest bar about 5.1x, highest about 19.7x; values read by eye from the figure).
compiler_and_flags: Benchmark Makefile: -O3 -std=c++11, plus -fopenmp -march=native (g++) or -qopenmp -xhost (icpc); the compiler and version used for the plotted numpy comparison are not stated (README only lists tested compilers: icpc 15/16/17, g++ 5.4-6.3, clang++ 3.8/3.9).
stars_or_usage: 205 stars, 52 forks; the transposition engine under TCL (springer13/tcl) and a dependency of TCCG
tradeoffs: Out-of-place only. Explicit AVX and ARM micro-kernels plus a scalar fallback (no explicit AVX-512 or IBM POWER kernels, listed as TODO; complex types not explicitly vectorized). Optional FFTW-style auto-tuning (hptt::MEASURE/PATIENT) costs plan-creation time; the default hptt::ESTIMATE uses a performance model. Supports float, double, complex and double complex, row- and column-major. C++11 library with C and Python interfaces (the Python benchmark script is Python 2 era).
caveats: The only named-baseline numbers on opened pages are against numpy.transpose, which is not one of the listed baselines (OpenBLAS, MKL, Eigen, BLIS), and the comparison is HPTT on 24 threads against a numpy copy whose thread count is not stated (numpy's copy is typically single-threaded), so the 5-20x range mostly shows multi-threaded bandwidth use. HPTT also applies alpha/beta while the numpy side only copies. The figures are images, so values are read by eye. The repo's C++ benchmark (benchmark/benchmark.cpp) compares only against an in-repo naive OpenMP reference transposition (transpose_ref, labelled 'TTC (ref)') and optionally the original TTC, not against Eigen or BLAS. benchmark/bw.png (paper Fig. 6) shows HPTT bandwidth against the system SAXPY and STREAM lines on Ivy Bridge, KNL, IBM Power7, AMD and ARM machines, not against a named library. The peer-reviewed paper (Springer, Su, Bientinesi, ARRAY 2017, arXiv 1704.04374, DOI 10.1145/3091966.3091968) reportedly also compares against Eigen's tensor transposition and TTC; its abstract (seen only as a search-engine snippet because arXiv and ACM are blocked in this session) says HPTT reaches on average 92%/102% of SAXPY/STREAM bandwidth on Ivy Bridge and remarkable speedups over Eigen. Those numbers were not opened and are not used above; a verifier who can open the paper should consider raising this to tier B and switching the baseline to Eigen tensor shuffle. Repository unmaintained since 2022. A transposition library is BLAS-adjacent rather than a BLAS/LAPACK routine, so the category is a loose fit.

name: TCCG / GETT (Tensor Contraction Code Generator)
language: Python (generator that emits vectorized C code)
baseline: TTGT (transpose-transpose-GEMM-transpose) tensor contraction built on Intel MKL sgemm/dgemm (the repo's default BLAS in config.cfg is MKL); TTGT is TCCG's own backend, not a third-party tensor library
workload: Dense tensor contractions from the repo's benchmark v0.1 (CCSD, AO2MO and intensli test cases, up to 6-D tensors, largest tensor 200 MiB), single and double precision, GFLOPS on one core; GETT versus LoG versus TTGT, and TCCG versus the best of CTF/naive (single) or CTF/TT/naive (double).
claimed_speedup: No numeric table; values read by eye from benchmark/GETT_LoG_TTGT.png. Single precision on one Haswell core: abcde-efbad-cf GETT about 20.5 GFLOPS vs TTGT about 15 (about 1.4x, derived from figure); abcdef-dfgb-geac GETT about 55.5 vs TTGT about 25 (about 2.2x, derived from figure). On compute-bound cases TTGT ties or beats GETT (for example abcd-aebf-fdec about 67 vs about 75 GFLOPS single precision). benchmark.png (Fig. 11): TCCG about 55 GFLOPS vs best-of(CTF, naive) about 13 on abcdef-dfgb-geac. README text only says GETT is 'especially outstanding' for bandwidth-bound contractions.
hardware: Single core of an Intel Xeon E5-2680 v3 (Haswell); ECC enabled, Intel SpeedStep and TurboBoost disabled
stars_or_usage: 40 stars; GETT is the contraction method behind TCL and the subject of ACM TOMS 2018 / arXiv 1607.00145
tradeoffs: Generator written in Python 2.7 that emits C with AVX2 (AVX-512 experimental; CUDA only for TTGT and LoG); needs Intel icc 15+ (g++ 4.8+ experimental), a BLAS such as MKL, and the HPTT library. GETT has a stated limitation: the product of free-index sizes of each input tensor must be a multiple of 24. Auto-tuning explores up to N candidate implementations at generation time (--maxImplementations). Parallel GETT only on the v0.2.0 branch per the changelog; the published benchmark is single-core.
caveats: No LICENSE file in the repository (raw LICENSE, LICENSE.txt, LICENSE.md and COPYING all returned 404 and GitHub shows none), so the code is reference-only even though the sibling HPTT is BSD-3-Clause. The TTGT baseline is the authors' own implementation (HPTT-style transposes plus MKL GEMM) rather than an independent library. Results are single-core, 2016-era hardware and compiler; figures are images, so values are read by eye and approximate. GETT does not win everywhere: on compute-bound contractions TTGT is on par or faster. benchmark.py also drives libtensor, TBLIS, CTF and Eigen scripts (with a hard-coded author path) but the README publishes only the GETT/LoG/TTGT and TCCG-vs-best-of-others figures. The peer-reviewed paper (Springer and Bientinesi, ACM TOMS 2018, arXiv 1607.00145) is not opened (arXiv, ACM and the author's PDF host are blocked); its abstract, seen only as search-engine snippets, reports up to 12.4x over existing approaches for bandwidth-bound contractions and up to 91.3% of peak on compute-bound ones; those numbers are not used above. Abandoned since 2017.

name: batmat (batched small-matrix linear algebra)
baseline: Intel MKL and OpenBLAS (per-matrix BLAS/LAPACK calls via the BLAS interface), BLASFEO
workload: Batches (depth 8) of small dense matrices, sizes 1 to 1024, for gemm, syrk, trmm, trsm, trtri, potrf, syrk-potrf, QR and others, single-threaded (OMP_NUM_THREADS=1, taskset -c 0), batmat interleaved SIMD kernels versus per-matrix calls of BLAS libraries, BLASFEO and Eigen; benchmark source only, no published results.
claimed_speedup: README gives no numbers: 'Batmat performs exceptionally well on matrices smaller than around 100x100 (that fit in the L2 cache), where it outperforms traditional scalar linear algebra libraries such as Intel MKL, OpenBLAS, and BLASFEO (especially for triangular or symmetric matrices).'
compiler_and_flags: GCC 14 or later required (Clang and ICX supported); SIMD flags come from the user's Conan profile (scripts/dev/profiles); benchmark target run with Google Benchmark --benchmark_min_time=0.1s, 3 repetitions, random interleaving. Actual flags of the author's runs are not published.
stars_or_usage: 3 stars; linear-algebra backend of the Cyqlone optimal-control solver (kul-optec/cyqlone)
tradeoffs: Data must be stored in an interleaved 'compact' layout (one SIMD lane per matrix of the batch), so it helps only when many same-sized small matrices are processed together (for example stages of an optimal control problem) and is not a drop-in replacement for single-matrix BLAS. Needs GCC 14+ (or Clang with the GSI-HPC simd library, or ICX), Conan and the guanaqo dependency. LGPL-3.0 licence. Routines include gemm, syrk, trmm, trsm, potrf, trtri and fused variants.
caveats: The README states a win over MKL, OpenBLAS and BLASFEO but publishes no numbers, no CPU model and no result files (docs/ holds only logos and Doxygen config). The benchmark sources exist (benchmarks/*.cpp, including benchmarks/mkl/potrf-mkl.cpp) and run the baselines as ordinary per-matrix calls (MKL dpotrf, guanaqo BLAS xgemm) rather than MKL's compact or batched APIs, so the comparison is batched-SIMD against non-batched calls. The Cyqlone paper (Pas and Patrinos, arXiv 2512.09058), whose abstract per a search snippet says batched routines 'significantly outperform BLAS and BLASFEO for the small matrices that arise in optimal control', and a Zenodo benchmark record could not be opened (arXiv and Zenodo blocked), so no numbers are recorded. Very new, 3 stars.

name: HipKittens (AMD) / ThunderKittens sibling
baseline: AITER (AMD hand-tuned assembly attention kernels); also Composable Kernel, PyTorch SDPA, Triton and hipBLASLt in other plots
workload: GQA non-causal attention backward pass on one AMD Instinct MI355X: batch 16, 64 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 128, sequence length 1024 to 16384, TFLOPS (repo's analysis/attn/bkwd plot).
claimed_speedup: analysis/attn/bkwd plot mi355x_gqa_non_causal_bkwd_plot.png: HipKittens 881 / 1007 / 1106 / 1155 / 1176 TFLOPS at sequence length 1024 / 2048 / 4096 / 8192 / 16384 versus AITER 300 / 351 / 375 / 384 / 389, Composable Kernel 368 / 428 / 447 / 463 / 465 and PyTorch SDPA 220 / 273 / 301 / 309 / 312; about 2.9-3.0x over AITER (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: hipcc from the ROCm 7.0 preview Docker image (rocm/7.0-preview:rocm7.0_preview_pytorch_training_mi35x_beta); BF16 GEMM Makefile uses -std=c++20 --offload-arch=gfx950 -DKITTENS_CDNA4 -ffast-math (attention Makefile flags not read); baselines run with 500 warmup and 100 repeat iterations (analysis/baselines/README.md).
hardware: AMD Instinct MI355X (gfx950, CDNA4); host CPU not stated; CDNA3 branch also covers MI300X/MI325X
stars_or_usage: 472 stars, 81 forks; MLSys 2026 paper; README says HK kernels landed in AMD AITER (March 2026) and AMD Transformer Engine (June 2026) as backends
tradeoffs: AMD CDNA3/CDNA4 GPUs only (MI355X/MI350X on main, MI300X/MI325X on the cdna3 branch), needs ROCm and hipcc. A tile-primitive DSL in C++ rather than a drop-in library: kernels are written per operation and shape configuration (matrix sizes are Makefile constants). Covers BF16/FP8/FP6 GEMM, MHA/GQA attention forward and backward, rotary and layernorm.
caveats: Baselines are AMD libraries (AITER, hipBLASLt, Composable Kernel) plus Triton and PyTorch, none of which are in the category's baseline list (oneDNN, cuDNN, XNNPACK, Eigen tensor), and this is a GPU kernel library, so it fits the category only loosely. The attention-backward win is large, but the same repo's BF16 GEMM plot (analysis/bf16_gemm/README.md, mi355x_bf16_gemm.json) shows parity with AMD's own libraries: at N=8192 HipKittens 1610 TFLOPS vs AITER 1591, hipBLASLt 1575, Triton 1091, Composable Kernel 504; HipKittens is slower than hipBLASLt at N=1024 (139 vs 168), 4096 (1413 vs 1433) and 16384 (1571 vs 1579). Baseline numbers were collected by the authors in October/November 2025 and the README warns the frameworks keep evolving; AITER now includes HipKittens kernels, so a re-run may differ. Plot values were read from PNGs (the GEMM numbers also appear in the repo JSON). The paper (arXiv 2511.08083, MLSys 2026) and the Hazy Research and AMD blogs could not be opened (hosts blocked), so their headline figures (for example 1.3-3x over Triton) are not used.

name: libxsmm-dnn
baseline: oneDNN (no comparison exists in this repository; the oneDNN comparison of the IPDPS 2020 paper belongs to LIBXSMM)
workload: Convolution, fully-connected, pooling and normalization drivers (tests/conv/run_convs.sh and friends) in f32/bf16/bf8 over ResNet-50, AlexNet, dcGAN, DeepBench, GoogLeNet, MaskRCNN, Overfeat and VGG layers, reporting FLOPS of the layer time; no external library measured.
claimed_speedup: None. The README only says the run_convs.sh command 'mimic[s] the performance of ResNet-50 inference' and that FLOPS and conv-layer time are shown, 'different from running inference end-to-end using a real framework'.
stars_or_usage: 14 stars; companion repository of LIBXSMM that holds the deep-learning operators and convolution drivers moved out of the main repo
tradeoffs: Reference implementation of DL primitives built on LIBXSMM's Tensor Processing Primitives (LIBXSMM as a git submodule, JIT-generated kernels); C sources; x86 focus (BF16/BF8 paths target AVX-512/AMX-capable Intel Xeons). Meant to demonstrate TPP usage rather than to be a general framework backend.
caveats: Fold into LIBXSMM (already listed): this repo is where LIBXSMM's DL layers now live, and it has no oneDNN numbers of its own (a grep of the repo's README, CI YAMLs and run_convs.sh found no oneDNN or MKL-DNN reference; the LIBXSMM README likewise has none). The IPDPS 2020 paper (Georganas et al., 'Harnessing Deep Learning via a Single Building Block') could not be opened (IEEE and Semantic Scholar blocked), so no numbers are recorded. The CI pipeline scripts/buildkite/libxsmm-tpp.yml names partition 'emr' and config 'intel-2022' but states no CPU model, so hardware is unknown. Tier D with 14 stars is below the usual notability bar for D records.

name: BesTLA (Neural Speed weight-only-quantized GEMM)
baseline: oneDNN (no BesTLA comparison exists); the parent project's claim is against llama.cpp (ggml) CPU kernels
workload: bestla_benchmark (bestla/bestla/ut/bestla_benchmark.cpp) prints GEMM Flops and per-core Flops for BesTLA's own AVX2/AVX512/AMX kernels (sgemm, u8s8 and s8s8 igemm, bf16); no external library is measured. End-to-end LLM inference is claimed only for Neural Speed as a whole.
claimed_speedup: None for BesTLA standalone. The parent Neural Speed README (a listed project) claims 'Up to 40x performance speedup on popular LLMs compared with llama.cpp', end-to-end LLM inference, not BesTLA's GEMM kernels alone.
compiler_and_flags: bestla/README.md: GCC >= 9 to compile, GCC >= 11 for best performance (MSVC >= 1930, oneAPI/DPC++ >= 2024.0); benchmark built with cmake -DBTLA_UT_BENCHMARK=ON -DBTLA_UT_ALL=ON -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
stars_or_usage: 352 stars for the parent intel/neural-speed (archived by Intel on 2024-08-30)
tradeoffs: Header-only C++ template library (Launcher, Parallel, GemmCore, Prologue, Epilogue, inspired by CUTLASS) with JIT kernels (kernel_jit*.h), x86 Intel only: AVX2, AVX_VNNI, AVX512F/BW/VNNI/FP16, AMX_BF16 and AMX_INT8, plus a SYCL directory. Weight-only quantization from INT1 to INT8, FP8, FP4 and NF4 with BF16/FP32 scales and fused GELU/SWISH/RELU/EXP/TANH epilogues; a hybrid-CPU thread pool the README says is 'much faster than OMP' (no numbers).
caveats: Component of the already-listed Neural Speed (this record points at the same repo URL and likely needs a paper: id or a duplicate decision). No standalone numbers against oneDNN or llama.cpp kernels exist in the repo: bestla_benchmark.cpp only prints BesTLA's own Flops, and docs/advanced_usage.md and neural_speed/core/README.md contain no comparison. The 40x claim is end-to-end and first-party (the backing Medium blog could not be opened, host blocked). Intel archived the repository on 2024-08-30 and points to intel-extension-for-pytorch as the alternative.
